Bachelor's thesis · 2022 · Politehnica University of Timisoara

Smart Home

A 3D-printed model house with a real alarm system inside it — motion, door contacts, climate and lighting, split across two microcontrollers.

Eng. Narcis Pantea — Robotics Engineer Design, electronics and firmware Faculty of Robotics Supervisor: Lect. Dr. Eng. Cristian Pop

What it does

Five behaviours, running continuously once the system is armed.

Access

Arms and disarms with a code

A 4×4 membrane keypad on the front wall. Press *, type the four-digit code, and the house switches state. The display confirms every step.

Intrusion

Sees movement inside

A passive infrared sensor watches the interior. If it detects motion while the system is armed, the alarm fires — buzzer, indicator LED and a message on the display.

Perimeter

Knows if a door is open

A magnetic reed contact reports whether the door is actually shut. The system refuses to finish arming until it is, rather than arming around an open door.

Climate

Reports temperature and humidity

A DHT11 sensor samples the room once a second. The readings go to the display and, over Wi-Fi, to a phone app with live gauges and history.

Lighting

Turns the lights on by itself

A photoresistor measures how much daylight reaches the room. Below a set threshold the indoor LEDs switch on without anyone asking.

The point

Every one of these is a physical measurement turned into a decision and then into an action — a sensor, a rule, an actuator. That loop is the whole project.

How it works

Two boards, deliberately separated. The Arduino Uno owns security and never depends on the network. The ESP32 owns everything that has to leave the house.

Three states, not two

An alarm that only knows on and off will happily arm itself around an open door. This one has a third state in between, and it will not leave it until the perimeter is actually closed.

Error Close the door.

This is what the display shows while the system is waiting in the middle state. It is not a failure message — it is the system telling you the one thing standing between you and an armed house.

Designing and printing the house

The model is not a box with parts glued in. It was drawn as a floor plan first, with the door and window openings the sensors would eventually watch.

The parts were printed in sections on a Prusa i3 and an Ender 5 Pro — 1.75 mm filament in, 0.04 mm layers out, on a 200 × 200 × 200 mm build volume. One section had to be extended after the fact, because the first print left no room to route the wiring behind the front wall once every sensor was in place.

On the phone

The ESP32 publishes three values to a Blynk dashboard: temperature, humidity, and the light reading that drives the lamps.

The platform is Blynk. It was chosen over the other options considered — IoT Cloud and PlatformIO among them — for one practical reason: it gives both a phone app and a desktop console without needing a server of its own, which for a one-person thesis project is the difference between finishing and not.

On the board, a BlynkTimer calls sendSensor() once a second. That function reads the DHT11 and the photoresistor and pushes three values up with Blynk.virtualWrite(). Nothing is polled from the other direction.

The two screens above are the same room at different moments: on the left, warmer and much more humid, with the lighting indicator lit; on the right, cooler, drier, indicator off. The widget labels were set in Romanian when the dashboard was built — Temperatura is temperature, Umiditate is humidity.

How a widget is bound, and how it changes

A widget is bound to a datastream, not to a pin — the datastream carries the virtual pin. Title, scale, label format, colour and which series a chart draws are all set here, in the app. The firmware only writes the right number to the right virtual pin, so the whole display could be rearranged without reflashing the board once.

Running on the bench

Before the electronics moved into the printed house, the same firmware and the same dashboard ran on a breadboard.

The finished model

Printed shell, acrylic cover, and every sensor mounted where the plan said it should go.

From the front, with the roof on. The wiring is deliberately left visible — this is a demonstration model, meant to be opened and explained, not a sealed product.

The clear shell keeps the whole system in view while it runs, so the alarm can be triggered and every part of the reaction — display, buzzer, LED — can be pointed at while it happens.

What I would change today

This was built in 2022, as a first serious embedded project. Four things I would do differently now.

Credentials do not belong in firmware

The Wi-Fi password and the cloud token were compiled straight into the sketch. They belong in a separate configuration file that never enters version control, with only an example committed alongside it.

One sensor is not evidence

A single PIR reading raises the alarm. Combining it with the door contact, the light level and a short time window would separate a real entry from a curtain moving in a draught.

A fixed threshold is a guess

The lighting switches at a hard-coded analogue value of 200. A baseline learned from the room over a few days would hold up across seasons instead of being tuned once, in one light.

Nothing was ever written down

The system has no log. Every state change and every trigger should be timestamped and stored, so that a false alarm at three in the morning can be explained the next day rather than argued about.
